Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Recognize anatomy pertinent to the diagnosis and management of distal radius fractures.
Identify the elements of a distal radius fracture that may benefit from surgical management.
Discuss conditions occasionally associated with distal radius fractures, such as median
neuropathy, forearm compartment syndrome, ulnar styloid fracture/rupture of the origin of
the radioulnar ligaments, and intercarpal ligament injury.
Summarize areas of debate with regard to the treatment of patients with a distal radius
fracture and areas in which additional experimental data may be useful to patients and
surgeons.

Fractures of the distal radius are common, particularly as individuals age, osteoporosis
develops, and individuals become less agile and more prone to falls.
Most distal radius fractures non-articular or minimally articular.
Angular alignment and shortening are key considerations.
Visible deformity (aesthetic concerns)
Restriction of forearm rotation
Limitation of flexion (for dorsally displaced fractures, which are more common)
Troubling pain persisting for more than 1 year is uncommon.
Wait more than 1 year before considering management for pain on the ulnar side of the
wrist.
Only consider surgical management if a correctable pathology is clearly causing most of
the symptoms (uncommon).
Symptoms of arthritis (radiocarpal or distal radioulnar) years or decades after a distal
radius fracture are uncommon; therefore, this is uncommonly a concern.
Partial articular fractures usually are shearing injuries.
Nondisplaced fractures can be managed nonsurgically and monitored for displacement.
Displaced fractures—Maintenance of articular alignment without surgical management may
be difficult.

Many can be managed similar to extra-articular fractures.

Displaced fractures (>2 mm)
May lose alignment even if they can be reduced with manipulation.
Consider potential central articular impaction
Associated with arthritis on imaging studies
Arthritic changes do not correlate with pain intensity and level of capability.
Specific management of wrist arthritis after a distal radius fracture is relatively
uncommon.
Subset of very fragmented, widely displaced fractures.

Fracture incidence in adults
22 per 10,000 individuals per year1

Incidence increases more rapidly in women.

A widely displaced fracture of the distal radius results in disruption via one of the following:

Somewhat conical

Vascular Anatomy
Radial artery (Figure 2)
Immediately radial to the flexor carpi radialis (FCR) tendon on the volar aspect of the wrist
The most common exposure of the distal radius is between the radial artery and the FCR,
opening the FCR tendon sheath volar and dorsal and retracting the FCR ulnarward.5
The radial artery rarely is transected during a high-energy, widely displaced fracture, and
the proximal end may be found within the fracture.6
Managed via ligation if the hand is well vascularized
Main artery courses radial and dorsal at the radial styloid
Branch to the superficial palmar arch crosses ulnarly over the FCR at the distal pole of
the scaphoid
Ulnar artery
Runs with the ulnar nerve on the ulnar side of the wrist
The extended carpal tunnel approach to the distal radius is between the contents of the
carpal canal and the ulnar nerve and artery.7

Median nerve
Deep to the palmaris longus tendon (if present; 85% of patients)
Palmar cutaneous branch
Separates approximately 5 cm proximal to the transverse wrist crease

Prominent on the volar radial wrist

At risk of spontaneous rupture after the following:
Nondisplaced or minimally displaced fracture of the distal radius9

linkage between the ulna and the radius must be disrupted via avulsion of the origin of

Scapholunate ligament complete rupture is strongly associated with a partial articular
shearing fracture of the radial styloid14 If associated with a complete articular or extra-
articular fracture, complete ruptures are uncommon, and debate exists with regard to
whether partially intact scapholunate ligaments benefit from specific management.12,16
Distinguishing whether a complete scapholunate ligament rupture is new or old may be
difficult. Surgical management of the scapholunate ligament is associated with longer
protection times and greater wrist stiffness. Repair may be associated with less future
arthritis; however, this is not well studied.

Injury Classification
Numerous classification systems
Conceptual rather than definitive
Limited agreement (reliability)17
Fernandez classification system and the AO Foundation/Orthopaedic Trauma Association
classification of distal radius fractures18 (Figure 4)
Type A/bending; extra-articular
Dorsal (Colles fracture)
Volar (Smith fracture)
Type B/shearing; partial articular
Dorsal (reverse Barton fracture)
Volar (Barton fracture)
Radial styloid (occasionally referred to a Chauffer fracture)
Type C/compression; complete articular fracture
Other types:
Fernandez separated the following types of fractures19:
Radiocarpal fracture-dislocations
Typically, radial styloid fracture and dorsal articular marginal shearing fracture.
Combined, high-energy fractures
A subset of very complex fractures, most of which currently are managed with the use
of a distraction plate20 and via ancillary fixation.
Overlapping fracture types
Approximately one-half of fractures primarily characterized by a volar shearing fragment
and volar subluxation of the radiocarpal joint are complete articular fractures.21
The dorsal articular fragment is fractured and rotated volarly.
This fragment may be stable, and the fracture may be missed.
Risk of dorsal displacement with the use of a buttress plate22
Most radiocarpal fracture-dislocations have a dorsal articular marginal shearing
component.23

Imaging Studies
Evaluation of an injured wrist should consider the potential for emergent, urgent, and
regional injuries that may influence management, including diagnostic assessment and
the timing of management. After a global patient assessment, the elbow, forearm axis,
and carpus should be evaluated for concomitant regional injury. A comprehensive
evaluation includes inspection for open injury; deformity; and signs of trauma, such as
ecchymosis or joint effusion. Palpation facilitates localization of injury; pain, deformity,
and crepitus may be appreciated during a careful physical examination. The clinical
examination will guide additional evaluation, including radiographic assessment and

advanced imaging studies, such as CT scans (Figures 8 and 9), which will aid in treatment
planning. In general, two or three radiographic views (AP or PA views and lateral views,
with or without oblique views) will facilitate appreciation of the fracture characteristics.
Identifying the critical fracture segments is important in determining management,
including surgical versus nonsurgical treatment options, surgical exposure, and optimal
fracture fixation methods. Occasionally, dynamic radiographs, such as traction views or
fluoroscopy, may supplement pre-management assessment. Intraoperative assessment,
such as arthroscopic visualization of the articular surface during fracture reduction and
repair, also may guide management. Video 2 reviews radiographic assessment of the
wrist and considerations for fracture reduction techniques.

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Minimally/Limited Displaced Fractures
Minimally displaced fractures include those with less than:
10° of dorsal angulation on a lateral radiograph (and limited fragmentation of the
metaphysis)
2 mm of ulnar positive variance (relative to the opposite wrist if uncertain)
2 mm of an articular step or gap
Unlikely to lose alignment25
Associated with good long-term comfort and capability with natural healing
4 to 6 weeks of immobilization
Below elbow cast
Velcro wrist splint
No fragmentation, limited displacement
Patients who wish to undergo less cumbersome immobilization and are likely to adhere to
restrictions.
Small risk of extensor pollicis longus rupture9

Individuals who elect to accommodate the following:
Visible deformity
Limited motion
For example, volar flexion with dorsal angular deformity
Loss of forearm rotation (difficult to predict, may take a long period to ensure it results
from deformity)
Small risk of pain from ulnocarpal impaction.
Surprisingly uncommon
Wait 1 year before considering ulnar-sided wrist pain to be a potential problem.
This pain is the last pain to resolve.
Recovery continues for more than 1 year.
Infirm/inactive individuals


Displaced Fractures
If good technique is used (including good anesthesia, good manipulation, and adequate
immobilization), repeat reduction and immobilization likely will not maintain
alignment.27 Evidence suggests that unstable fractures are no more likely to stay in place
with the use of an above elbow splint or cast.28 The best approach appears to be a
single, technically adequate reduction attempt—using repeat manipulation only if
technical inadequacies, such as inadequate anesthesia, occurred—followed by below
elbow immobilization, a discussion on tolerance of deformity, and observation of the
fracture based on deformity tolerance preference. For example, a patient who would
elect to undergo surgical treatment if the fracture lost some threshold of alignment is
monitored more closely. A patient unlikely to elect to undergo surgical treatment can be
monitored less frequently (Video 3).

Good evidence shows that pinning results in long-term outcomes comparable to those
of volar plate fixation of the distal radius.29 This likely results from the relative
accommodation of slight to moderate deformity of the distal radius (pinning results in
poorer radiographic outcomes) and some of the disadvantages of plate fixation
(including tendon irritation by the implant). Given that pinning can be performed in the
office with the use of inexpensive implants, pinning may be a high-value treatment
option and merits additional research and consideration.
External fixation is associated with limited ability to control alignment in isolation.
Historically, external fixation often was used for neutralization or for additional support
with ancillary pin fixation or bone grafting of a metaphyseal defect. Nonbridging external
fixation was popular for a period. The major advantage of placing pins in the distal
radius fragment is better control of alignment. This is only possible in simple articular or
non-articular fractures. If patients can move their fingers and wrist well, pin infection is a
common complication, usually observed approximately 1 month, and oral antibiotic
agents can be used to manage the infection and maintain the fixator in place for the full
6 weeks (Video 4).

Pitfalls and Pearls
Distal radius fractures are common. Consider contributing causes, such as fall risk and
metabolic conditions.
Recognize fracture characteristics associated with potential adverse outcomes: articular
depression (die-punch injury), volar lunate facet and volar rim fractures (carpal translation),
pre-reduction displacement (inherent instability)
Align treatment options with patient priorities, taking care to gently correct common
misconceptions.
Help patients move and use their arm confidently during recovery. Painful activities considered
healthful may be counterintuitive.
If patients have more intense pain and are more incapable than expected, monitor for
compartment syndrome and neuropathy; however, unhelpful thoughts (worst-case thinking,
fear of painful movement) and feelings of worry or despair should be anticipated as the more
common problems.
